questions.prompt: What does “signal flow” describe?
choices: The path a signal takes through a system
How much reverb is on a signal
The kind of cable a signal travels on
questions.explanation: Signal flow is the path audio takes from its source through inputs, processing, routing, and outputs.

questions.prompt: A wireless receiver shows microphone signal, but the mixer input meter shows nothing. What troubleshooting approach best follows signal flow?
choices: Check the cable and routing from the wireless receiver to the mixer input
questions.explanation: Follow the signal in order. The wireless receiver shows signal, so the mic and transmitter are working; the problem is somewhere between the receiver output and the mixer input.

questions.prompt: A DAW is showing no microphone signal. Which should you check first?
choices: Whether the correct input device and track input are selected
Whether the track is panned center
Whether the master fader is at 0 dB
Whether the track has EQ on it
questions.explanation: Correct I/O is fundamental: the DAW must use the intended device and the track must listen to the correct input.

questions.prompt: You want to record through an audio interface, but the DAW is still using the computer’s built-in microphone. What needs to change?
questions.explanation: The DAW records from whichever input device is selected in its audio settings. Choose the interface there, then pick the corresponding input on the track.

questions.prompt: Before recording into a DAW track, what usually needs to be enabled on that track?
questions.explanation: Record-arming tells the DAW which track should receive and record the incoming signal.

questions.prompt: You press Record and the playhead moves, but no new audio appears on your microphone track. What is a likely cause?
choices: The master fader is at 0 dB
questions.explanation: Only record-armed tracks capture new audio. If the track isn’t armed, the DAW runs without recording onto it.

questions.prompt: Which control should you use first to get a healthy microphone level entering a mixer or interface?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets the level entering the channel. Faders are normally used afterward to balance signals in a mix.

questions.prompt: A microphone is extremely quiet at the channel input. Which control is the most direct first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets how strongly the mic signal enters the channel. Faders come later, for balancing a signal that’s already healthy.

questions.prompt: In a digital recording system, what is the main problem with reaching or exceeding 0 dBFS?
questions.explanation: 0 dBFS is the digital ceiling. Trying to go beyond it causes clipping.

questions.prompt: You’re doing a test recording before the show, and the input meter hits the red clip light during the loudest passages. What should you do?
choices: Turn down the input gain and test again
Turn down only the main fader
questions.explanation: Since this is a test, fix it now: turn down the input gain and record another test. Don’t wait until the real take to find out.

questions.prompt: You’re recording a live concert and a mic starts clipping a little on the loudest passages. What should you do?
choices: Pull the gain down just slightly, and note the time and how much you changed it
Leave it alone; fixing clipping in post works fine
Pull the gain down a lot right away to be safe
Stop the recording and restart it
questions.explanation: We prefer not to change gain mid-concert unless it’s really clipping. If you do, change it just a little and log the time and amount, so it can be corrected in post.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest difference between mono and stereo audio?
choices: Mono uses one channel; stereo uses two channels
Mono is quiet; stereo is loud
Mono is analog; stereo is digital
Mono uses XLR; stereo uses USB
questions.explanation: Mono is one channel. Stereo uses two channels, normally left and right.

questions.prompt: You are recording one microphone into Input 1. What track format is usually appropriate?
questions.explanation: One microphone feeding one interface input is a mono source, so a mono DAW track is normally appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which microphone type requires 48V phantom power?
questions.explanation: Condenser mics need 48V phantom power (rare exceptions, like tube mics with their own power supply). Dynamic mics work either way, and ribbon mics must never get it.

questions.prompt: You connect a condenser microphone and the input meter shows nothing. Which setting is worth checking first?
questions.explanation: Condenser microphones need 48V phantom power to work. With it off, you get no signal.

questions.prompt: Which kind of microphone must never be given phantom power?
questions.explanation: Phantom power can damage ribbon mics, so keep 48V off on their channels (rare exception: some modern active ribbons need it). Condensers need it; dynamics don’t care either way.

questions.prompt: What is a basic job of an audio interface?
choices: Connect music hardware — mics, instruments, speakers — to the computer
Automatically mix and master a song
Replace the need for a DAW
questions.explanation: An audio interface connects analog audio sources and outputs with the computer and commonly contains preamps and converters.

questions.prompt: When you record into a computer through an audio interface, where does the microphone plug in?
choices: An XLR input on the interface
questions.explanation: Microphones plug into the interface’s XLR inputs. On many interfaces those are combo jacks that also take a ¼-inch plug.

questions.prompt: A recording call begins at 7:00 p.m. What best matches the course idea of being “on time”?
choices: Send a message at 7:05 saying you are parking
questions.explanation: For recording work, being on time means being ready to work at the scheduled time, not merely arriving at that moment.

questions.prompt: A problem will make you late for a recording call. What best matches the course professionalism standard?
choices: Wait until after the recording to mention it
Only tell another student after the start time
questions.explanation: Reliability includes communicating early, before a scheduling problem becomes a larger problem.

questions.prompt: Your group finishes a camera activity. What best matches “finish the job”?
choices: Restore default settings and return the gear and batteries
Leave as soon as your clips are recorded
Leave the camera on so the next group is ready
Keep the SD card in your bag to check later
questions.explanation: The job isn’t done until the gear is reset and returned. The next person should find it ready to use, with batteries back where they belong.

questions.prompt: Who is the monitor mix mainly for?
questions.explanation: Monitors help performers hear themselves. Their mix can be different from the audience’s Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: Why might a monitor mix be different from the mains?
choices: Performers may need different things emphasized than the audience does
questions.explanation: Performers often need a custom balance so they can hear what helps them perform, while mains are mixed for the audience.

questions.prompt: A singer asks for more of their own voice on stage without making it louder for the audience. What should you adjust?
questions.explanation: The monitor mix is for the performer and can be adjusted independently from the audience mix.

questions.prompt: What is the basic difference between an active speaker and a passive speaker?
choices: An active speaker has amplification built in; a passive speaker needs an external amplifier
Active speakers use XLR; passive speakers use USB
questions.explanation: Active/powered speakers contain an amplifier. Passive speakers need an external power amplifier.

questions.prompt: You’re setting up a passive speaker. What does it need between the mixer and the speaker?
questions.explanation: A passive speaker has no amplifier inside, so the mixer’s output has to go through a power amplifier first.

questions.prompt: What is the safe basic power rule for speakers?
choices: Speakers ON last and OFF first
Speakers ON first and OFF last
Speakers must stay on all day
questions.explanation: Turning speakers on last and off first helps prevent loud pops and surprises from upstream equipment.

questions.prompt: You are shutting down a live sound system. Which should happen first?
choices: Turn off every microphone before anything else
questions.explanation: Speakers and amplifiers should be turned off first during shutdown to reduce the chance of loud pops.

questions.prompt: What is feedback in a live sound system?
choices: Sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone and loops through the system
A DAW exports a WAV file
A passive speaker receives amplifier power
questions.explanation: Feedback occurs when amplified sound returns to a microphone and is amplified again in a loop.

questions.prompt: A vocal mic starts to squeal whenever the singer walks in front of the main speakers. What’s the best first fix?
choices: Keep the mic behind the speakers and pointed away from them
Turn up the mic’s input gain
questions.explanation: Feedback happens when the speakers’ sound gets back into the mic. Keeping mics behind the speakers and aimed away from them breaks the loop.

questions.prompt: Aperture/iris is primarily a control related to what?
choices: How much light enters through the lens
questions.explanation: Aperture/iris changes the lens opening and therefore affects how much light reaches the camera sensor.

questions.prompt: You change the aperture from F4 to F5.6. What happens?
choices: Less light gets in, because the opening is smaller
More light gets in, because the opening is bigger
questions.explanation: A higher f-number means a smaller lens opening, so F5.6 lets in less light than F4.

questions.prompt: Shutter speed is part of which general camera task?
questions.explanation: Shutter speed affects exposure and also changes how motion is rendered.

questions.prompt: What happens to moving subjects when you use a much slower shutter speed?
choices: They look sharper and more frozen
questions.explanation: A slower shutter exposes each frame for longer, so movement smears into motion blur. The image also gets brighter.

questions.prompt: What is the usual tradeoff when you raise a camera’s gain/ISO?
choices: The image gets brighter but noisier (grainier)
The image gets darker but sharper
questions.explanation: Gain/ISO brightens the image electronically, and that adds visible noise, or grain.

questions.prompt: White balance is mainly used to control what?
questions.explanation: White balance tells the camera how to interpret color under different lighting. Kelvin is commonly used to set color temperature.

questions.prompt: A shot looks unnaturally blue or orange under the room lighting. Which setting is most directly related?
questions.explanation: White balance controls how the camera interprets color under the current lighting.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest purpose of focus?
choices: Make the intended subject appear sharp
questions.explanation: Focus determines what distance/subject appears sharp in the image.

questions.prompt: Which stereo technique uses two directional microphones with capsules very close together and angled apart?
questions.explanation: XY is a coincident stereo technique: the microphone capsules are placed very close together and angled apart.

questions.prompt: Why does an XY recording usually hold up well when it’s summed to mono?
choices: The capsules are nearly in the same spot, so sound reaches both at the same time
questions.explanation: With the capsules together there’s almost no time difference between the two mics, so combining them avoids the phase cancellation a spaced pair can have.

questions.prompt: Which technique is commonly described as a spaced pair of microphones?
questions.explanation: A/B uses two microphones spaced apart to capture stereo information.

questions.prompt: ORTF is best described as which kind of setup?
questions.explanation: ORTF is a near-coincident stereo technique: two cardioid microphones about 17 cm apart, angled 110° from each other.

questions.prompt: In the current basic stereo-recording activity, how should the two microphone input gains generally be treated?
choices: Set to matching values unless there is a specific reason not to
One must always be at minimum
The right side must always be louder
questions.explanation: The activity calls for matching gains so the stereo pair begins from a balanced setup.

questions.prompt: For a basic two-channel stereo recording, how are the channels normally panned?
questions.explanation: A basic stereo pair needs distinct left and right channels so the spatial information is preserved.

questions.prompt: Both stereo mic tracks recorded cleanly, but playback sounds like everything is in the middle. What’s the likely setup mistake?
choices: The input gain is too high
questions.explanation: With both channels panned center, the left/right differences collapse into the middle. Pan one hard left and the other hard right.

questions.prompt: In the X32 activity, buses are used for what important task?
questions.explanation: Buses can create separate mixes, such as Monitor 1 and Monitor 2, that differ from the Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: What does Sends on Fader help you adjust on the X32?
choices: How much of each input is sent to a selected bus
questions.explanation: Sends on Fader lets the faders represent channel send levels into the selected bus, which is useful for monitor mixes.

questions.prompt: What is Dante Controller mainly used for in these activities?
choices: Routing network audio transmitters to receivers
questions.explanation: Dante Controller provides the routing matrix used to connect Dante transmit and receive channels.

questions.prompt: What role does Dante Virtual Soundcard (DVS) play?
choices: It lets a computer send/receive audio channels on the Dante network
questions.explanation: DVS allows computer audio software to use Dante network channels as audio I/O.

questions.prompt: In a Dante routing matrix, what are you creating when you click the intersection between a transmitter channel and receiver channel?
questions.explanation: The matrix intersection connects a transmitting Dante channel to a receiving Dante channel.

questions.prompt: In Dante, what does a transmitter channel do?
questions.explanation: Transmitters send audio onto the Dante network and receivers pick it up. The routing matrix connects a transmitter channel to a receiver channel.

questions.prompt: Why is signal-flow thinking especially useful in a live-looping rig?
choices: Several devices and effects must be connected in the correct order
questions.explanation: A live-looping setup may pass through instruments, effects, a looper, vocal processing, and speakers, so following the signal path is essential.

questions.prompt: In our recording activities, what’s a healthy peak level to aim for?
questions.explanation: Peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS leave headroom for louder moments while staying well above the noise.

questions.prompt: Your test recording peaks around −38 dBFS. What does that tell you?
choices: It’s too quiet; raise the input gain
The track needs to be stereo
questions.explanation: −38 dBFS is far below the −12 to −6 target, so the recording will be noisy once it’s turned up. Raise the input gain and test again.

questions.prompt: Why not record as loud as possible, just under 0 dBFS?
choices: A louder moment in the performance could clip
Louder files take more disk space
questions.explanation: Performances often get louder than the soundcheck, so leave headroom for the loudest moment.

questions.prompt: Which microphone type is rugged and handles loud sources, like guitar amps, especially well?
questions.explanation: Dynamic mics are the tough, loud-source workhorses. Condensers are more sensitive, and ribbons are fragile.

questions.prompt: You’re recording a quiet solo piano recital and want a detailed sound. Which microphone type is the usual choice?
questions.explanation: Condensers are sensitive and detailed, which suits quiet acoustic music.

questions.prompt: Before patching a ribbon microphone into a channel, what should you check?
choices: That the channel is panned hard left
questions.explanation: Phantom power can damage ribbon mics, so make sure 48V is off first (rare exception: some modern active ribbons need it).

questions.prompt: Which connector is the standard for microphone cables?
questions.explanation: XLR is three-pin, locking, and balanced: the standard for microphones.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between a ¼″ TS plug and a ¼″ TRS plug?
choices: TS has two contacts (tip, sleeve); TRS has three (tip, ring, sleeve)
TS is for speakers only; TRS is for mics only
TS is digital; TRS is analog
questions.explanation: Count the black rings: TS has one, TRS has two. TS carries unbalanced signals like a guitar; TRS carries balanced line signals or stereo headphones.

questions.prompt: An interface input accepts either an XLR plug or a ¼″ plug. What is that input called?
questions.explanation: A combo jack has an XLR socket with a ¼″ hole in the middle, so it takes either kind of plug.

questions.prompt: Which plug is most likely on a pair of laptop earbuds?
questions.explanation: Phones and laptops use the small 3.5 mm (⅛″) plug, usually stereo.

questions.prompt: Your meters look fine. Why record a short test and listen back anyway?
choices: Meters can’t reveal problems like distortion, noise, or the wrong mic
A test raises the sample rate
The DAW won’t record without one
questions.explanation: Meters only show level. Listening back is how you catch distortion, noise, a dead channel, or the wrong mic before the real take.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to test every important input, output, and playback source for a live event?
questions.explanation: Line-check everything before the event. Problems found during the show are much harder, and much more public, to fix.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between a DAW project and a deliverable?
choices: Project: your editable session. Deliverable: the finished export.
They’re two names for the same file.
Project: the finished export. Deliverable: your editable session.
Project: only the raw WAVs. Deliverable: the DAW file.
questions.explanation: The project keeps everything editable. The deliverable is the finished file someone else receives, like a WAV. Keep both.

questions.prompt: Before you start recording, what should you know about your files?
choices: How long the final mix will be
questions.explanation: Know which folder or drive the project and audio are going to, so nothing gets lost or saved somewhere you can’t find.

questions.prompt: After exporting your mix, why keep the project too?
choices: So you can reopen it and make changes later
The export won’t play without it
It makes the export sound better
questions.explanation: The export is fixed. The project is what lets you go back and change the mix without starting over.

questions.prompt: What does Solo do on a DAW track?
choices: Plays only that track (and any other soloed tracks)
questions.explanation: Solo isolates a track so you can hear it alone. Mute is the one that silences a track.

questions.prompt: You want a finished WAV of your mix to hand in. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Exporting (bouncing or rendering) turns the mix into a finished audio file, like a WAV.

questions.prompt: Which control places a track’s sound between the left and right speakers?
questions.explanation: Pan sets left-right position. Faders set level.

questions.prompt: In a DAW, where do you choose which audio device (like your interface) to record from?
questions.explanation: The input and output device is chosen in the DAW’s audio settings. Each track then picks an input on that device.

questions.prompt: What does the A/D converter in an audio interface do?
choices: Turns the analog signal into digital audio the computer can record
questions.explanation: A/D means analog-to-digital. The D/A converter does the reverse for your speakers or headphones.

questions.prompt: Which order matches basic live-sound signal flow?
questions.explanation: Sound starts at the source, is picked up by the mic, is mixed, is amplified if needed, and comes out of the speakers.

questions.prompt: A recording clipped during the loudest chord. Can you fix it by turning the track down afterward?
choices: No, the distortion is already recorded
Yes, lowering the fader removes it
Yes, exporting as WAV removes it
Yes, panning it center removes it
questions.explanation: Once a signal clips, the distortion is part of the recording. Prevent it with input gain and headroom before you record.

questions.prompt: You have eight tracks and want to record only the vocal. What should be record-armed?
questions.explanation: Arm only the track you mean to record onto, so you don’t record over or add to the others by accident.

questions.prompt: You record with a stereo mic pair. How many input channels does that use?
choices: It depends on the sample rate
questions.explanation: A stereo pair is two mics feeding two inputs: one for left, one for right.

questions.prompt: If you hear an audio engineer say “gain before fader,” what are they probably talking about?
choices: Set a healthy input level first, then use faders to balance
Keep every fader above its gain knob
Raise the faders before touching gain
Gain and faders do the same job
questions.explanation: Input gain gets the signal to a healthy level at the start of the channel. Faders come afterward, for balancing the mix.

questions.prompt: A groupmate is stuck setting up the interface while you wait. What best fits the course’s idea of professionalism?
choices: Help them, or ask how you can help
Wait until they figure it out
Start packing up your own things
Work on something for another class
questions.explanation: Reliability includes helping your group get the whole job done, not just your own part.

questions.prompt: Which three settings make up the exposure triangle?
questions.explanation: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO/gain together set how bright the image is.

questions.prompt: Why shoot a recital in manual exposure?
choices: So the brightness doesn’t shift on its own during the performance
Manual exposure is required to record audio
Autofocus only works in manual exposure
questions.explanation: In auto, the camera keeps re-guessing brightness as lights and movement change. Manual keeps it where you set it.

questions.prompt: The shot is too dark, and you don’t want more noise or more motion blur. What should you change?
questions.explanation: Raising gain adds noise and slowing the shutter adds blur. Opening the aperture lets in more light without either.

questions.prompt: What does frame rate measure?
choices: How many frames are recorded each second
How many pixels are in each frame
questions.explanation: Frame rate is frames per second (fps), like 24, 30, or 60.

questions.prompt: You’re shooting at 30 fps. Which shutter speed is a common starting point?
questions.explanation: A shutter about twice the frame rate (1/60 at 30 fps) gives natural-looking motion. It’s also what the Cameras activity used.

questions.prompt: You change the shutter from 1/60 to 1/250. What happens to the image?
choices: It gets darker, and motion looks sharper and choppier
It gets brighter, with more motion blur
questions.explanation: A faster shutter lets in less light per frame and freezes motion, which can look choppy in video.

questions.prompt: Which Kelvin setting matches warm indoor (tungsten) light, like the Cameras activity’s default?
questions.explanation: Around 3200 K suits warm indoor light. Around 5600 K suits daylight.

questions.prompt: Why might you switch to manual focus for a fixed recital shot?
choices: Autofocus can hunt or jump to the wrong subject
Manual focus makes the image brighter
questions.explanation: Autofocus may wander when someone walks through the frame or the light changes. Manual focus stays where you set it.

questions.prompt: What does framing refer to?
choices: What’s in the shot and where it sits
questions.explanation: Framing is composition: what the shot includes, and where the performers sit in it.

questions.prompt: Which change brightens the image but adds grain?
questions.explanation: Gain/ISO brightens electronically, and the tradeoff is noise.

questions.prompt: In a system with passive speakers, what comes between the mixer and the speakers?
questions.explanation: Passive speakers have no amplifier inside, so the mixer feeds a power amplifier, which drives the speakers.

questions.prompt: What does a DI box do?
choices: Converts an instrument or line signal into a balanced mic-level signal
Records audio to an SD card
questions.explanation: A DI lets a keyboard, guitar, or playback device connect to a mixer’s mic input over a balanced cable.

questions.prompt: Who normally hears the mains?
choices: Nobody; mains are only for recording
questions.explanation: Mains are the audience mix. Monitors are the performer mix.

questions.prompt: You’re powering up a PA. Which should be turned on last?
questions.explanation: Speakers on last, off first, so pops from other gear powering up never reach them.

questions.prompt: Which change is most likely to reduce feedback?
choices: Point the mic toward the speaker
questions.explanation: Feedback is a loop. Lowering the level, or moving the mic away from the speakers, breaks it.

questions.prompt: Before you raise any levels, what should you know about the mixer’s outputs?
choices: What feeds the mains, the monitors, and the recording
How loud the room can get
questions.explanation: Know where each output goes before turning things up, so nothing surprises the audience, the performers, or the recording.

questions.prompt: Copying the finished recital files to the archive belongs to which core skill area?
questions.explanation: Organizing, backing up, and archiving files is data management & archiving.

questions.prompt: Editing and mixing a recital recording after the concert falls under which core skill area?
questions.explanation: Work done on the recording afterward, like editing and mixing, is post production.

questions.prompt: What are the ORTF spacing and angle?
choices: About 1 m apart, pointing straight ahead
About 17 cm apart, pointing straight ahead
questions.explanation: ORTF uses two cardioid mics about 17 cm apart, angled 110° from each other.

questions.prompt: Compared with XY, what’s a typical tradeoff of an A/B spaced pair?
choices: A wider, more spacious image, but weaker mono compatibility
A narrower image with perfect mono compatibility
It can’t be used for classical music
questions.explanation: Spacing the mics widens the image, but the time differences between them can cause phase problems when summed to mono.

questions.prompt: In XY, how are the two microphones placed?
choices: Capsules as close together as possible, angled apart
One above the stage, one at the back of the hall
questions.explanation: XY is coincident: the capsules sit together and point in different directions.

questions.prompt: Your stereo recording leans left even though the mics are placed symmetrically. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the two input gains match
questions.explanation: If one channel has more input gain than the other, the image pulls toward that side.

questions.prompt: On the X32, what does a bus master fader control?
choices: The overall level of that bus’s mix
questions.explanation: Each channel sends some level into the bus; the bus master sets the level of the whole mix, like one monitor.

questions.prompt: With Sends on Fader active for Bus 1, you raise the vocal channel’s fader. What changes?
choices: How much vocal goes to Bus 1
The vocal level in Main L/R
questions.explanation: In Sends on Fader mode, the channel faders control sends into the selected bus, not the main mix.

questions.prompt: The mains sound fine, but the singer’s monitor wedge is silent. What’s a sensible first check?
choices: The vocal’s send to that monitor bus, and the bus master
questions.explanation: Since the mains work, the input is fine. The problem is in the monitor path: the send into the bus, the bus master, or the bus output.

questions.prompt: How does a wireless mic’s signal get into the mixer?
choices: The mic transmits to its paired receiver, and the receiver’s output connects to a mixer input
The mic sends audio straight to the speakers
The mixer’s 48V powers the wireless link
The mic connects to the mixer over USB
questions.explanation: The transmitter and receiver must be paired; then the receiver’s output is patched into a mixer channel like any other source.

questions.prompt: What does Dante do?
choices: Carries many channels of audio over a computer network
questions.explanation: Dante sends many audio channels over standard network cabling instead of one cable per channel.

questions.prompt: Computer A plays music that Computer B should record over Dante. Which one is the transmitter?
questions.explanation: The device sending the audio is the transmitter. Computer B receives it.

questions.prompt: On a Dante-connected computer, which audio device does the DAW use to reach the network?
questions.explanation: DVS appears to the DAW as an audio device. Dante Controller is the routing software, not an audio device.

questions.prompt: Computer B’s DAW shows no signal from Computer A, and DVS is running on both. What should you check in Dante Controller?
choices: That A’s transmit channels are routed to B’s receive channels
That the network cable is XLR
questions.explanation: Audio only flows on Dante once a transmitter channel is subscribed to a receiver channel in the routing matrix.

questions.prompt: In the looping rig, which device combines everything and produces sound in the room?
questions.explanation: The B205D is the mixer and speaker. Every path ends there.

questions.prompt: In the looping rig, which channel is tested last because it’s the most feedback-prone?
questions.explanation: The open headset mic is the one that can feed back, so it’s added last, and it’s the first to turn down if feedback starts.

questions.prompt: Why must the RC-30 and MicroKorg 9V adapters never be swapped?
choices: They have opposite polarity, which can damage the device
Swapping them erases the loop memory
questions.explanation: The Korg adapter is center-positive and the Boss adapter is center-negative. The wrong one can damage the device.

questions.prompt: You hear live guitar, but no loop plays back. Following the rig’s signal path, what should you check?
choices: G3X balanced out → RC-30 mic in, and RC-30 output → Channel 2
questions.explanation: The loop path runs from the G3X balanced output through the RC-30 to Channel 2, so check each link in that path.
